alerts.headline: Coastal Flood Watch issued November 23 at 2:34PM PST until November 26 at 2:00PM PST by NWS Eureka CA
alerts.description:
* WHAT...For the Coastal Flood Warning, High astronomical tides
and moderate surf will cause moderate flooding in low lying
areas along the Redwood and Mendocino Coast. Up to two feet of
saltwater inundation above ground level is possible in low lying
areas near shorelines and tidal waterways. Between 8.25 and 8.75
MLLW is expected at the Arena Cove tide gauge. At the Crescent
City tide gauge 9.5 to 10.0 feet MLLW is predicted.

* For the Coastal Flood Watch, High astronomical tides and
breaking waves of 25 to 30 feet are expected on Wednesday may
cause major flooding in low lying areas along the Redwood and
Mendocino Coast. Up to two feet of foot of saltwater inundation
above ground level is possible in low lying areas near
shorelines and tidal waterways.

* WHERE...Coastal Del Norte, Southwestern Humboldt and Coastal
Mendocino Counties.

* WHEN...For the Coastal Flood Warning, from 9 AM to 1 PM PST
Tuesday. For the Coastal Flood Watch, from Wednesday morning
through Thursday afternoon at high tide. Saltwater inundation
will be possible 1 to 2 hours before and after high tide.

* IMPACTS...Several coastal roads may be closed. Low lying
property and some critical infrastructure will be inundated.
These impacts will include, but not limited to highway 101 near
Crescent City and Hwy 1 in low lying areas along the Mendocino
coast. Shoreline erosion will occur.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...Larger surf is expected to bring more
significant impacts on Wednesday.
alerts.instruction:
A Coastal Flood Warning means that flooding is occurring or
imminent. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert
for rising water and take appropriate action to protect life and
property.

Feet Above Ground is locally defined as feet above the Highest
Astronomical Tide or HAT.

alerts.headline: Coastal Flood Warning issued November 23 at 2:34PM PST until November 24 at 1:00PM PST by NWS Eureka CA
alerts.description:
* WHAT...For the Coastal Flood Warning, High astronomical tides
will cause major flooding in low lying areas mainly around
Humboldt Bay. Up to 3 of saltwater inundation above ground level
is possible in low lying areas near shorelines and tidal
waterways. Between 10.3 and 11.0 feet MLLW at the North Spit
tide gauge is predicted. For the Coastal Flood Watch, High
astronomical tides and large surf may cause major flooding in
low lying areas along the Redwood Coast. Up to 2.5 foot of
saltwater inundation above ground level is possible in low lying
areas near shorelines and tidal waterways.

* WHERE...Northern Coastal Humboldt County.

* WHEN...For the Coastal Flood Warning, from 9 AM to 1 PM PST
Tuesday. For the Coastal Flood Watch, from Wednesday morning
through Thursday afternoon. High tide is at 11:09 AM on
Wednesday and 11:56 AM on Thursday at the Humboldt Bay North
Spit tide gauge. Saltwater inundation will be possible 1 to 2
hours before and after high tide.

* IMPACTS...Several coastal roads may be closed. Low lying
property and some critical infrastructure will be inundated.
These impacts will include, but not limited to, roadways and
houses in King Salmon and the Arcata bottoms. This may also
include highway 101 near College of the Redwoods and Hwy 255
near the Mad River Slough. Shoreline erosion will occur.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...The water levels from this are expected to
exceed the water levels seen in January of 2026 that caused
significant flooding in King Salmon.

* WHAT...For the Wind Advisory, south winds 20 to 35 mph with gusts

difficult, especially for high profile vehicles.

strongest late Tuesday morning through Tuesday afternoon.

profile vehicles. Use extra caution.

inflatable holiday decorations that could be blown around or damaged
by the wind.

alerts.description:

southwest facing beaches.

National Weather Service Eureka CA
106 AM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

* Strong south wind will gradually build Monday and peak Tuesday 
  with gusts over 45 mph ahead of a strong cold front.

* Period of heavy rain along Tuesdays front with greatest rain 
  focused in Mendocino County with 1 to 2 inches most likely. 
  Additional rain later in the week.

* High astronomical tides with water levels already increased by El 
  Nino, will coincide with strong Pacific storm systems, likely 
  generating record breaking Coastal Flooding Monday(11/23) through 
  Thursday(11/26) at high tide. Greatest risk will be Tuesday and 
  Wednesday.


&&

.SYNOPSIS...Conditions will remain cool and cloudy as another, 
stronger storm system approaches Northwest California Monday. South 
winds are forecast to increase Monday afternoon with strong winds 
and heavy rain Tuesday alongside the potential for record breaking 
coastal inundation around high tide. 


&&

.DISCUSSION...Cool and cloudy conditions remain across the area with 
valley fog mostly inhibiting widespread valley frost early this 
morning. This system will bring increasing southerly winds gusting 
up to 25 mph by early afternoon with stronger winds through the 
evening hours. A few weak showers will stream along shore today with 
little expected rainfall. 

Strong winds will continue to increase into Tuesday as the front 
approaches. Models show that a low level jet of high winds 
(generally 55 to 65 kts) is expected over the Del Norte and Humboldt 
through Tuesday. These winds aloft have the potential to mix down to 
the surface, especially along the immediate coast from about Cape 
Mendocino and north into Oregon. The NBM suggest most likely wind 
gusts in exposed areas of Humboldt and Del Norte of just around 45 
mph. REFS ensemble shows a 70% chance of gusts at the coast of 45 
mph, and generally less than a 20% chance for 55 mph gusts. 
Deterministic models suggest some higher winds around Crescent City, 
but the need for a High Wind Warning remains marginal. Regardless, 
45 mph usually results in minor wind damage and small power 
outages. The potential for higher winds is generally less for most 
areas of Trinity, Mendocino and Lake counties. However, these areas 
will still most likely see gusts near 40 mph in exposed areas. Such 
speeds will be enough to increase the risk for power outages and 
significantly increase storm surge potential during the King Tides 
(refer to the 'Coastal Flooding' section for more info).

The higher rainfall potentials have decreased, but overall rain with 
the system will still be notable. NBM 24-hour rainfall totals (from 
Tuesday morning to Wednesday morning) indicates a 75 to 85 percent 
chance of 0.5 inches or greater for Del Norte, northern Humboldt and 
central Trinity (mostly along the Trinity River Valley). There is 
about a 65 to 85 percent chance for NBM 24-hour rainfall totals of 
1.5 inches or greater for most of southern Humboldt, Mendocino and 
northern and western Lake counties with closer to 0.5 to 1 inch 
expected for southeastern Lake. There is about a 60 to 80 percent 
chance of NBM 24-hour rainfall totals of 2 inches or more for the 
King Range in Humboldt County and the higher terrain areas of 
southwest Mendocino County. The greatest potential for heavy rain 
will be along the Mendocino Coast. Such rain amounts could cause 
minor to moderate small stream flooding, especially in streams that 
are tidally influenced. That said, CNRFC guidance shows rivers still 
have a ways to go before river flooding will be a concern. As a 
result, no significant river impacts are expected. The warm nature 
of the system will limit any snow concerns to above 5000 feet. 

Showers will persist early Wednesday alongside at least moderate 
south winds. Another cold front has the potential to pass by the 
region early Thursday. This front will bring another period of 
slightly weaker gusty southerly winds. Most ensemble models have 
generally weakened this front with only 0.2 to 0.6 inches of rain 
now most likely, all near shore north of Cape Mendocino. /JLW &
/JHW


&&

.AVIATION...06Z...VFR conditions have persisted all evening,
outside of the interior valleys where fog and stratus have
developed, with showers remaining far offshore. At most, ceilings
around 10 kft have been passing over the area. Strong southerly 
winds will gradually build in through the day Monday. Near shore, 
gusts will near 25 kts with winds around 40 kts at 2 kft 
generating some minor low level wind shear. Ceiling will generally
remain VFR, no lower than 7 kft. Conditions will gradually 
deteriorate into Tuesday as rain builds. /JHW


&&

.MARINE...Southerlies continue to build overnight into Monday as an 
approaching cold front enter the area. A steep, mid-period swell 
will keep seas steep regardless of winds, lasting through Monday 
evening. Small craft advisories have been issued to cover for the 
hazards of this wave group before winds become the primary threat to 
mariners beginning early Monday afternoon. Widespread gale to storm 
force winds in the northern waters will build by late Monday night 
and peak during the day Tuesday. This will cause extremely chaotic 
seas and mariners are recommended to remain in port during this 
period. Warnings have been issued for each respective zone to cover 
the increasing threats from this weeks coming storms. 

Later this week after the initial storm passage, a moderate to large 
mid-period swell arrives to the waters at around 17-19ft @ 17sec. 
This swell will likely warrant a Hazardous Seas Warning, yet this 
will become more clear after more deep water buoy observations 
become available. Strong southerlies return Wednesday late morning 
lasting through Thursday early monring most likely promoting further 
gale warnings for the northern waters, yet confidence on coverage 
and timing remains low as of now. Expect additional NW swells and 
southerly winds through the coming week into next weekend as the 
storm track remains set over NW CA and the coastal waters. 


&&

.COASTAL FLOODING...High astronomical tides continue to grow 
this week peaking Tuesday through Thursday. Astronomical tides at 
the North Spit tide gauge reached 9.04ft Sunday(11/22) which is 
around 1.3ft above the standard modeled value of 7.7ft. The highest 
tides are expected in the late morning to midday hours through this 
period. 

The tidal anomaly has been reading consistently over 1.2-1.5 feet 
due to greater thermal expansion as warmer than normal ocean 
temperatures exist off the coastline due to El Nino. Storm surge 
from strong and persistent southerly winds and large breaking waves 
of 20-25 feet caused by the incoming storms will likely add an 
additional 1 to 1.5 ft Tuesday and Wednesday. These two factors 
(warm water + storm surge) have the potential to occur 
simultaneously, creating a total tide anomaly of 2.0 to 3.0 feet. 
Minor flooding around Humboldt Bay (water levels above 8.8 ft MLLW) 
is certain with moderate to major flooding likely during high tide 
each day through Friday of the coming work week. The highest 
astronomical tides for November are between 11/24 and 11/26 with 
each day reaching above 8.4 ft. Should the 1.5 ft anomaly remain, 
which is most likely, ~10 ft tide levels are expected. If the storm 
surge materializes as expected, the water levels could break the 
current record tide level of 10.37 ft MLLW set earlier this year in 
January. Storm surge is difficult to predict, but given the magnitude 
of winds on Tuesday, peak tides of 11 feet may be possible. 

Outside of Humboldt, the large swell expected late Tuesday into 
Wednesday could bring significant beach erosion and waves may wash 
over low lying areas of HWY 1 and HWY 101 along the coast at high 
tide. Impacts are also possible near Shelter Cove, Centerville 
Beach, and other exposed areas away from HWYs. 

A Coastal Flood Warning has been issued for Monday from 7am to 12pm 
around high tide in Humboldt Bay. Coastal Flood Watches have been 
issued for the entire NW CA coastline beginning Tuesday morning and 
lasting through Thursday's high tide. The time frame 2 hours before 
to 2 hours after high tide will very likely be switched to coastal 
flood warnings, especially for the Humboldt Bay area, during next 
week. Please prepare as best you can for this very likely record 
breaking event.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Sacramento CA
139 PM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

For additional details on weather and expected impacts over the
next 7 days, please visit weather.gov/sto/briefing.

.KEY MESSAGES... 

 - Mostly dry weather and near seasonable temperatures through
   Tuesday; Valley fog chances return overnight into Tuesday AM

 - Next weather system is trending weaker although rain, light
   high elevation mountain snow, and breezy southeast winds are 
   still on track Tuesday PM - Wednesday AM

 - Return to dry and seasonable weather with additional Valley fog
   chances Thanksgiving Day into the early weekend; Light Shasta 
   County showers remain possible
 
 - Flood Warning in effect through 4 PM Thursday for coastal
   flooding and erosion potential for the Delta vicinity

&&

.DISCUSSION...

...Today... 

While dense fog is beginning to dissipate across the area this 
morning, some reduced visibilities will likely continue into the 
early afternoon in the Valley. In areas where fog/low clouds 
linger, forecast high temperatures are expected to fall a few 
degrees short. Lower clouds will be less prevalent elsewhere, but 
a gradually approaching offshore weather system will introduce 
some cloud cover to these areas. Regardless, dry weather and near 
to slightly below normal temperatures and light winds look to 
persist today into Tuesday. Increasing cloud cover and winds 
overnight may limit another round of overnight Valley fog, but 
probabilities for visibility less than 1/2 mile are currently 
forecast at 40-60% for most of the Valley and Delta. 

...Tuesday-Wednesday... 

The next weather system will move into the area Tuesday 
afternoon/evening into Wednesday. Periods of light to moderate 
rainfall, light high elevation mountain snow showers, and breezy 
south- southeasterly winds are anticipated as the system builds 
in. Heaviest precipitation is currently expected Tuesday evening 
into early Wednesday morning with Valley showers then dissipating 
by midday Wednesday and mountain showers decreasing through the 
afternoon. Precipitation totals of 0.25"-0.5" are forecast for the
Delta, Valley, and foothills through Wednesday. Snow levels are 
expected to remain relatively high, around 6000 to 7000 feet 
throughout the event with heaviest snowfall forecast for locations
north of the Interstate 80 corridor. Minor travel delays and 
slick roads will be possible at pass level for commuters and 
holiday travelers over the Tuesday- Wednesday timeframe. 

As the system builds in, breezy south-southeast winds are 
forecast with gusts of 15 to 30 mph in the lower elevations and 
gusts of 20 to 40 mph over the Sierra Crest. With these increasing
winds alongside peaking King Tides this week, a Flood Warning has
been issued through 4 PM Thursday for the Delta vicinity due to 
coastal flooding potential. Moderate impacts from coastal flooding
and erosion are anticipated for low-lying areas throughout the 
Delta and vicinity.

...Thanksgiving Day-Friday...

As the midweek system ejects eastward by late Wednesday, a period
of amplifying ridging looks to build in across the end of the 
week. This will usher in another period of drier weather and 
warming temperatures for the Thanksgiving holiday and into the 
early portions of the following weekend. Daytime highs in the 
upper 50s to mid 60s are forecast for the Valleys/Foothills and 
40s to 50s for the mountains. While the broader drying weather 
pattern is on track for much of the area, some light rain shower 
potential will linger across Shasta County Thursday and Friday as 
progressive systems eject toward the Pac NW. Despite this, current
probabilities for rainfall > 0.1" are only forecast at 10-20%. 

...Next Weekend...

Some ensemble uncertainty continues to permeate the late extended
forecast period. In general, the late week ridge is expected to 
breakdown over the weekend, but timing differences persist at this
time. As a result onset of impacts from the next weather system 
remains fluid. Ensemble guidance is in broad agreement that a more
active weather pattern looks to arrive across the weekend, likely
continuing into the following week. While details will vary in 
the lead up, potential for additional periods of rain, mountain 
snow, and breezy to gusty winds are looking likely at this time. 

&&

.AVIATION...

LIFR conditions with visibility in fog down to 1/4SM or less 
through 19Z for terminals in the Delta, Southern Sacramento Valley
and northern San Joaquin Valley. Conditions are expected to 
improve to VFR/MVFR after 19Z. Prevailing VFR conditions for KRDD 
and KRBL. Tonight into Tuesday, LIFR conditions with visibility in
fog down to 1/4SM for terminals in the Delta, Southern Sacramento
Valley, and northern San Joaquin Valley through at least 16z; 
visibility should begin to improve between 16z and 18z as surface 
winds increase. Surface winds will be less than 10 kts and 
variable through 16z, then will increase up to 20 kts in the 
northern San Joaquin Valley and over higher mountain terrain after
16z. Otherwise, southerly winds up to 12 kts throughout the 
forecast period.

&&

.STO WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service San Francisco CA
1240 PM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

...New SHORT TERM, LONG TERM...

.KEY MESSAGES...
Updated at 1239 PM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

 - Major to extreme coastal flooding this week

 - Impactful storm brings rain and gusty winds Tuesday evening into
   Wednesday morning 

 - Drier conditions for Thanksgiving 

 - Wet weather returns for the upcoming weekend

&&

.SHORT TERM...
Issued at 1239 PM PST Mon Nov 23 2026
(This evening through Wednesday)

Satellite imagery reveals high clouds across the region with patches 
of lingering low clouds in the inland regions. Much of these clouds 
are expected to dissipate as we go further into the afternoon. 
Today is a dry and cool day, and it would be a good day to make 
sure drains and gutters are cleared before the rain arrives 
Tuesday. High temperatures will range from the middle 50s to the 
lower 60s across the lower elevations, into the middle 40s to 
lower 50s in the higher elevations. 

An area of persistent troughing across the waters south of Alaska is 
spinning up an intense upper level low across the waters of the 
north-central Pacific Ocean, which will approach the Pacific 
Northwest and drag a plume of moisture along with it. That's been 
known for the last several days. What wasn't clear was some of the 
finer details about how the moisture plume would set up. Some of the 
earlier projections depicted a more zonal moisture plume, which 
would flow more west to east and increase the potential rainfall 
totals across the region. Now, it's becoming pretty clear that the 
moisture plume will be more meridional, aligned more in a south to 
north direction. The latter orientation has led to a less impactful 
system than what earlier forecasts had suggested as the position of 
the deformation zone puts the most intense impacts to our north 
across the Pacific Northwest and into the North Coast. 

The current forecast is for a cold front associated with that upper 
level low to come through the region Tuesday evening into Wednesday 
morning. The latest update brings rain into the North Bay sometime 
Tuesday evening, coming into the Bay Area Tuesday night, and 
entering the Monterey-Salinas area after midnight early on Wednesday 
morning. Rain totals range from 0.5-1.2" in the North Bay, up to 
1.5" in the Sonoma coastal ranges, 0.5-1" in the San Mateo Peninsula 
and down into the Santa Cruz Mountains, around 0.2-0.5" in the 
interior regions of the Bay Area, 0.1-0.25" in the southern Monterey 
Bay region, 0.25-0.5" in the Santa Lucia range, and 0-0.2" in the 
interior Central Coast. Of note, there's still a fair bit of 
uncertainty regarding the evolution of this front as model output 
from the RRFS appears to bring the front slower into the Bay Area 
and weakens the front before it arrives in the Central Coast, while 
HRRR model output brings the showers intact into the Central Coast. 
Widespread wind gusts of 25 to 35 mph are expected across the region 
Tuesday afternoon through Wednesday morning with winds calming 
behind the front. Favored areas in the coastal North Bay, near the 
San Francisco and San Pablo Bays, and within Altamont Pass could see 
gusts up to 45 mph. There's also a chance for isolated thunderstorms 
in the coastal waters and within the North Bay as the front passes 
through and within the post-frontal environment. Lift over land will 
be limited by cool surface temperatures and the lack of solar 
heating overnight, but the abnormally warm coastal waters may 
support some strong cells with threats of localized heavy downpours, 
locally gusty winds, and lightning. Highs will begin to rise into 
the lower to middle 60s across the lower elevations. 

Major coastal flooding concerns continue through the next couple of 
days as the combination of high astronomical tides (the first in a 
sequence of "King Tides" around November through January) and surge 
residual from thermal expansion and storm surge effects leads to 
flooding concerns across low-lying areas of the Bayshore areas and 
the Pacific Coast. A Coastal Flood Warning for the San Francisco and 
San Pablo Bays, and a Coastal Flood Advisory for the Pacific coast, 
remain in effect through Thursday's high tide cycle. In addition, 
incoming large swell will lead to high breaking waves of 20 to 30 
feet on Wednesday, with a High Surf Warning out for the entire 
day. See the BEACHES section for more details.

&&

.LONG TERM...
Issued at 1239 PM PST Mon Nov 23 2026
(Thanksgiving Day through next Sunday)

As the system clears out late Wednesday, the Thanksgiving holiday 
itself and the Friday afterward should be generally dry, with an 
incoming ridge helping to warm the inland valleys into the middle to 
upper 60s.

The next chance for rain arrives for the upcoming weekend into the 
early part of next week. The persistent troughing south of Alaska 
will spit out another low pressure system that travels across the 
Pacific and approaches the West Coast. This will bring another plume 
of moisture into the region. Uncertainty over the specific details 
remains high. For the period between Saturday morning and Monday 
morning, NBM guidance for the rain total at downtown San Francisco 
suggests an 80 percent chance for rain totals between 0.1 and 1.8 
inches, and a 50 percent chance for rain totals between 0.5 and 1.3 
inches. Beyond the seven day outlook, a cursory analysis of the 
ensemble model means and cluster analysis suggests that the trend 
has been towards a stronger system coming into the West Coast, 
although anything further requires more confidence in the forecast 
this far out than what the science can support. 

&&

.AVIATION...
(18Z TAFS)
Issued at 1008 AM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

High confidence of VFR conditions prevailing through the TAF period 
excluding STS and LVK as fog and LIFR conditions slowly retreat from 
those terminals by 19Z. Winds are mainly out of the NE and SE with 
little variation through the TAF period. Ceilings are forecast to 
remain high as another round of rain nears.

Vicinity of SFO...High confidence of VFR conditions prevailing through the TAF 
period. Low confidence of low cloud development over the terminal at 
this time. The winds remain southeasterly and likely to increase 
near the end of the TAF period as the front approaches. 

SFO Bridge Approach...Low clouds impacting approach through 19Z.

Monterey Bay Terminals...VFR conditions are expected to persist through the TAF 
period. High confidence of light ESE winds through the remainder of 
the TAF period with an increase of light-moderate winds and high 
clouds at the end of the TAF period as the front approaches.

&&

.MARINE...
(Today through Saturday)
Issued at 1008 AM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

Strong to near gale southerly breezes expand from north to south
this morning through tomorrow, building rough to very rough seas
Tuesday into Wednesday. Hazardous conditions for small craft are
expected as a result. Frequent gale force gusts are likely Tuesday
morning and afternoon north of Point Reyes; elsewhere, infrequent
gale force gusts are expected. Moderate to heavy rainfall will
sweep from northwest to southeast Tuesday afternoon through
Wednesday morning with up to a 20% chance for thunderstorms. Seas
will begin to abate Thursday; however, rough seas will prevail
across the outer waters.

&&

.BEACHES...
Issued at 317 AM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

Coastal flooding will be a major impact this week. The combination
of king tides, storm surge, and thermal expansion from warm El
Nino waters will bring the tide to near record territory. A 
Coastal Flood Advisory is in effect for the San Francisco Bay 
until 6 AM PST Monday, at which point it will be upgraded to a 
Coastal Flood Warning through 4 PM Thursday. A Coastal Flood 
Advisory is also in effect for the Pacific Coast through 4 PM Thursday.
At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide is expected to be 2.2
ft above normal (8.0 ft MLLW) at 9:25 AM Monday, 2.6 ft above 
normal (8.4 ft MLLW) at 10:05 AM Tuesday, 2.8 ft above normal (8.6
ft MLLW) at 10:49 AM Wednesday, 2.4 ft above normal (8.2 ft MLLW)
at 11:38 AM Thursday, 1.7 ft above normal (7.9 ft MLLW) at 12:31 
PM Friday, and 2.2 ft above normal (8 ft MLLW) at 1:28 PM 
Saturday. These predictions include up to 1.6 ft of surge that 
will enhance the astronomical tide and flooding threat. High tide 
varies up to 90 minutes earlier or later along the Pacific Coast 
and through the San Francisco Bay, respectively.

Dangerously large breaking waves of 20 to 30 feet will be present
at Pacific Coast beaches Wednesday. Dangerously large breaking
waves can overpower swimmers, pulling people into the sea from
beaches, jetties, and rocks resulting in significant physical
injury and increasing the risk of drowning. Everyone should remain
out of the water due to life-threatening surf conditions. Stay off
of jetties, piers, and other waterside infrastructure and never
turn your back on the ocean! Hazardous beach conditions will 
linger at least through Sunday as another westerly swell train 
arrives. These conditions will coincide with King Tides and up to 
1.6 ft of surge, bringing water and waves farther up the beach 
than normal, restricting escape from beaches and coastal areas.

Flynn/Sarment

.KEY MESSAGES...
1. Dense fog advisory remains in effect through 11AM this 
morning for the San Joaquin Valley from Merced County to Delano.

2. Light rain and snow showers are possible Tuesday night into 
Wednesday morning with a low probability of any meaningful 
accumulation. 

3. A ridge of high pressure will build back into our area
through the Thanksgiving holiday.

.DISCUSSION...
A ridge is building over our region and will lead to warming
temperatures as we progress through the next couple of days.
Today the probability of temperatures exceeding 60 degrees is
very low only at around 5 to 20% across much of the San Joaquin
Valley, excluding localized areas such as Bakersfield with
higher probabilities. Temperatures will warm significantly by
the middle of the week with the probability of temperatures
exceeding 65 degrees on Wednesday at around 65 to 80%. In
addition to warming temepratures, fog currently remains in place
through much of the area and visibilities are as low as a
quarter mile. With the ridge building fog will continue to
remain possible after today. Current modeling is indicating
reductions in visibility across much of the valley tomorrow, 
and foggy conditions could move back in place by the end of this
week as a stronger ridge moves into the area. More details will
be provided about the fog potential as we progress closer to the
events.

By the middle of this week a weak trough will influence our 
weather and precipitation will move off the Pacific Ocean. There
is a possibility of light rainfall and snowfall in our area
Tuesday night into early Wednesday morning. Any precipitation
that does occur will be light in nature with only a 10 to 25%
chance of a tenth of an inch of rainfall across the northern
portion of our forecast area (the southern portion has
probabilities of almost 0%). A stronger ridge will move into our
area by the end of next week leading to above average
temperatures. By Saturday of next week the probability of
temperatures exceeding 65 degrees is around 55 to 70% in the 
northern valley and 80 to 95% in the southern valley. 

In terms of the long range forecast models indicate that the
ridge of high pressure in place early this coming weekend will 
weaken and move out of the area as we move into the end of this
coming weekend and into early the next week. There will 
therefore be a cooling trend and higher chances for 
precipitation as we move into the long term. The probability of 
at least a tenth of an inch of rainfall is above 50% by Monday 
and Tuesday of next week with many weather models picking up on 
a strong system moving in off the Pacific Ocean in that 
timeframe. The Climate Prediction Center (CPC) has us in a 50 to
60% chance for above normal temperatures and 50 to 60% chance
for above normal precipitation in the 6 to 10 Day Outlook.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Los Angeles/Oxnard CA 
226 PM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

.SYNOPSIS...23/115 PM.

Mild and dry conditions are expected into Tuesday except for some
cold overnight temperatures. Light rain is possible again Tuesday
night into Wednesday along the Central coast. Thanksgiving and 
Friday will be warm and dry. A cooling trend will begin over the 
weekend.

&&

.SHORT TERM (TDY-THU)...23/209 PM.

For the most part this will be a dry week with increasing offshore
flow and warming temperatures. The main caveat to that being
Tuesday night when the tail end of a storm moving into the Pac NW
and approaches SLO County. Models have backed off quite a bit on
rain chances there and any rain amounts would be very light and 
with very minimal impact. Clouds will eventually cover most of the
area Tuesday night into early Wednesday morning but sunny skies 
expected the rest of Wednesday.

In the meantime, offshore gradients are expected to be increasing
this week, starting Tuesday with gusts to around 30 mph from  
Santa Clarita and the surrounding mountains through the 126 
corridor and into the Oxnard plain, as well as the northwest San 
Fernando Valley. Winds expected to remain below advisory levels.

The return of offshore flow will start a warming trend that will
last through the week, conveniently peaking on Thanksgiving.
However, winds will increasing as well, possibly enough for some 
low end wind advisories in the above areas. The warmest 
temperatures will be at the coast and in the coastal valleys with 
highs in the upper 70s to mid 80s. The higher valleys and interior
areas will be cooler which is typical in offshore conditions.

.LONG TERM (FRI-MON)...23/225 PM.

Dry weather will continue at least through Saturday, though
temperatures will be cooling, especially for coast and valleys as
pressure gradients trend strongly onshore in response to the next
storm system moving into the Pac NW. That system will move through
the area mostly on Sunday. Most areas will get at least some light
rain, but more so along the Central Coast where up to an inch
could fall, especially the northern portion. Rain amounts south of
Pt Conception will be quite a bit less, likely under a half inch.

At least one more storm is expected next week, around Tuesday with
the possibility of 1-3 inches in upslope areas.

&&

.AVIATION...23/1709Z.

At 1600Z at KLAX, there was no marine layer nor an inversion.

Overall, high confidence in majority of 18Z TAFs as VFR conditions
are expected through the period.

The only exception will be KPRB where timing of dissipation of 
IFR CIGs this morning could be +/- 1 hour of current 18Z forecast 
and only moderate confidence in return of VLIFR conditions

through the period. No significant easterly wind component is
expected.

&&

.MARINE...23/114 PM.

For the Outer Waters, moderate to high confidence in current
forecast. Today through Tuesday, high confidence in winds and seas
remaining below Small Craft Advisory (SCA) levels. From Tuesday
night through Thursday night, high confidence in combination of
Small Craft Advisory (SCA) level winds and seas. Seas during this
period will peak between 14 and 18 feet on Wednesday and Wednesday
night. For Friday through Saturday, high confidence in winds
remaining below SCA levels, but a 60-80% chance of SCA level seas. 

For the Inner Waters north of Point Sal, moderate to high
confidence in current forecast. Today through Tuesday, high
confidence in winds and seas remaining below SCA levels. For
Tuesday night through Thursday night, high confidence in
combination of SCA level winds and seas. Seas during this period
will peak between 13 and 16 feet on Wednesday. For Friday through
Saturday, high confidence in winds remaining below SCA levels, but
a 40-60% chance of SCA level seas. 

For the Inner Waters south of Point Conception, moderate to high
confidence in current forecast. Today through Tuesday night, high
confidence in winds and seas remaining below SCA levels. For
Wednesday, there is a 50-60% chance of SCA level winds across the
western half of the Santa Barbara Channel and a 30-40% chance of
SCA level seas. For Thursday, there is a 50-70% chance of SCA
level northeast winds from Ventura to Santa Monica and a 40-60%
chance of SCA level seas. For Friday through Saturday, high
confidence in winds and seas remaining below SCA levels.

&&

.BEACHES...23/123 PM.

A large, long period, west swell will move into the coastal
waters on Tuesday and peak on Wednesday and Thursday. This large
swell will combine with very high tides to bring significant surf
to the area as well as significant coastal flooding.

The highest surf and most significant coastal flooding issues are
expected across the Central Coast as well as the beaches of
Ventura county. Elsewhere, the surf and coastal flooding issues
are a bit less, but still concerning. 

Please check out LAXCFWLOX for the latest details about all of the
current advisories and warnings in effect.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service San Diego CA
1158 AM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

.SYNOPSIS...
Dry conditions expected through Saturday. Today and Tuesday will see 
a few degrees of warming, Wednesday could see a minor cool down west 
of the mountains, before a more noticeable warm up for Thursday and 
Friday. Weak to locally moderate Santa Ana winds are expected for 
Thursday and Friday. Precipitation chances could return early next 
week, with low confidence in details. Widespread coastal flooding is 
expected this week due to King Tides and increased surf.

&&

.DISCUSSION...FOR EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA INCLUDING ORANGE...
SAN DIEGO...WESTERN RIVERSIDE AND SOUTHWESTERN SAN BERNARDINO
COUNTIES...

A few showers occurred overnight and early this morning mostly over 
San Diego and Orange County. North Island and Point Loma saw the 
highest rainfall totals at 0.14", further north and inland totals 
were 0.10" or less. Dry conditions are expected for the rest of the 
day through the rest of the week. Highs today will be a few degrees 
warmer than Sunday, with an additional 3-5 degrees of warming into 
Tuesday. 

The transient ridge that is currently over the Western United States 
will get pushed east Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning by an 
upper level low pressure system. This upper level low is not 
expected to bring impactful weather to the area. Conditions will 
stay dry with just a minor cooling west of the mountains. 

For Thursday, guidance has a ridge building back over California and 
the aforementioned trough to our east. There still remains some 
uncertainty in the position of the upper level low, but guidance 
continues to indicate the pressure gradient will turn offshore. The 
projected offshore surface gradient has trended slightly weaker 
compared to yesterday, increasing the chances for mainly weak 
Santa Ana winds to develop. Guidance from the CW3E West-WRF has
trended slightly higher chances for weak Santa Ana winds and 
slightly lower chances for weak to moderate Santa Ana winds. Wind 
gusts look to peak in the mountains, foothills, and passes at 35 
to 45 mph, with gusts to 45 mph confined to wind prone locations. 
The pressure gradient is most offshore on Thursday, which is when 
the strongest winds will be. In addition to winds, temperatures 
will peak Thursday and Friday. High temperatures will be 5 to 15 
degrees above average, with the warmest conditions on Friday. West
of the mountains, highs will be in the mid to upper 70s to 
mid-80s. 

By Saturday, most ensemble solutions have a trough of low pressure 
starting to push the ridge to our east. This will bring a few 
degrees of cooling for Saturday compared to Friday. By Sunday, there 
remains a spread of solutions of where the low will be but 60% of 
ensemble members continue to indicate the trough moving into 
Northern California with the other 40% showing more zonal flow. The 
troughing solutions are the ones most likely to bring us light 
precipitation in Southern California. The current forecast follows 
the NBM with chances of precipitation Sunday. A general troughing
pattern looks to prevail for much of next week, which has the 
potential to bring periods of additional precipitation, cooler 
conditions, and westerly winds for the first week of December. 

&&

.AVIATION... 
231800Z...FEW-SCT clouds based 4500-8000 ft MSL remain present 
across San Diego and the mountains/foothills this afternoon, but 
should gradually dissipate into the afternoon/evening. Shower 
activity has largely wound down as well, though a few showers remain 
off the coast in the lee of the Channel Islands. Overall, VFR 
conditions will prevail throughout the forecast period.

&&

.MARINE...
No hazardous marine conditions are expected through Tuesday.

A large, long period west swell will arrive Wednesday afternoon 
and build into Thursday, bringing combined seas of 8-12 feet. 
Northwest winds briefly reach 20-25 kt in the outer coastal waters
near San Clemente Island Wednesday afternoon and evening. The 
combination of large seas and breezy winds will create conditions 
hazardous to small craft. With this, a Small Craft Advisory has been 
issued for the outer waters from late Wednesday morning through late 
Thursday morning. Seas begin to wane Thursday afternoon, falling 
below 10 ft by Thursday evening.

&&

.BEACHES...
Morning high tides will increase this week, and have already reached 
7.73 feet (MLLW) on Monday morning at La Jolla. Highest tides will 
occur Tuesday through Thursday at 7.9-8.3 feet, peaking on 
Wednesday. These forecast tides have been adjusted 1.1-1.2 feet 
above baseline astronomical predictions based on trends in recent 
observations, and will likely break the all time tidal records 
recently set in late October. 

Background surf on top of the tides will remain around 2-5 feet 
through Wednesday morning, but an incoming west swell of 8-9 ft at 
18-19 seconds arrives late Wednesday into Thursday. This 
will generate large breaking waves of 6-8 feet on Thursday, with 
sets of 10-12 feet on exposed west-facing beaches. Surf lowers to 3-
6 feet on Friday. With this, a High Surf Advisory has been issued 
for San Diego County as the west-northwest swell will focus the 
higher surf on the west-facing beaches.

The combination of forecast record high tides and elevated surf will 
bring moderate to locally major coastal flooding during Tuesday 
morning's high tide. A Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect 
through early Tuesday morning. King Tides Tue-Thu combined with 
elevated to high surf bring major coastal flooding, with locally 
extreme flooding expected during Thursday morning's high tide. A 
Coastal Flood Warning remains in effect from Tuesday morning through 
early Friday afternoon.

&&

.SKYWARN... 
Skywarn activation is not requested. However weather spotters are
encouraged to report significant weather conditions.


&&

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Medford OR
955 AM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

.PREV DISCUSSION... /Issued 349 AM PST Mon Nov 23 2026/ 

..Updated AVIATION discussion for 18Z TAFs...

KEY MESSAGES...

* Coastal flooding remains a point of emphasis through much of the
  week ahead. A combination of King Tides and storm surge could
  push seawater into low-lying areas along the coast. For today, a
  Coastal Flood Advisory covers some initial concerns. A Coastal
  Flood Warning in place for Tuesday through Thursday addresses
  more widespread potential for coastal flooding. Please see the
  COASTAL AND BEACH HAZARDS section below.

* Slightly warm temperatures and chances for coastal showers are
  present today. Initial gusty winds develop along the coast as
  well as in the Shasta and eastern Rogue valleys.

* A warm front will bring some rainfall to areas west of the
  Cascades. Widespread gusty winds are expected. Hazardous winds
  are forecast for the Oregon coast south of Charleston, in the
  Shasta and eastern Rogue valleys, and in Lake County. Snow
  levels of 4500-5500 feet should keep snow off most highways.

* A second warm front will bring more rainfall and gusty winds
  late Wednesday into Thanksgiving day. Most rainfall is expected
  along the coast, with lighter rainfall inland. Snow levels of
  8000 feet or higher will limit snowfall to the highest peaks and
  ridgelines. Post-frontal showers may continue into Friday.

* After a pause in activity on Saturday, more rainfall is possible
  on Sunday. While snow levels lower somewhat, chances for wintry
  impacts remain low at this point.

DISCUSSION...The week starts off with a low pressure system 
approaching the Oregon coast but with its moment being slowed by a 
developing upper ridge. That ridge will keep precipitation out of 
most areas this morning, with a few showers possible along coastal 
areas. South to southeast winds start to increase this afternoon, 
which will bring gusty winds to coastal highlands, the Shasta 
Valley, and the southern Rogue Valley. Some light showers may push 
inland over Josephine and Douglas counties. This evening, hazardous 
winds develop for coastal areas south of Charleston. For areas 
farther east, some elevated winds are the only activity of note 
today.

The upper ridge shifts eastward on Tuesday and allows a tight 
pressure gradient around an upper low to push inland. A warm front 
will bring precipitation generally west of and along the Cascades, 
with the highest amounts over Curry County and the Mount Shasta 
region of Siskiyou County (Including Weed, Mount Shasta City, 
Dunsmuir, and McCloud). Snow levels look to be at 5000-6000 feet for 
Tuesday afternoon and evening, keeping most wintry weather to higher 
peaks in Siskiyou County. Areas around Crater Lake and Diamond Lake 
may see a couple inches of snowfall. Most areas will see elevated 
winds on Tuesday, with hazardous winds continuing along the coast 
south of Charleston, the Shasta Valley, the eastern Rogue Valley, 
and central Lake County. Please see NPWMFR for more details about 
these expected conditions.

Also on Tuesday, a combination of King Tides and especially strong 
winds over the ocean will make coastal flooding and high surf 
significant concerns that will continue through Thursday. For anyone 
living along the coast or planning to visit coastal areas early this 
week, please see the COASTAL AND BEACH HAZARDS discussion below as 
well as CFWMFR for more details about these uniquely hazardous 
conditions.

Precipitation and winds ease on Wednesday, with daytime highs 
forecast to be about 5 degrees above normal for most areas. Another 
warm front looks to bring more rainfall on Thursday, although model 
guidance shows some uncertainty for how far inland rain will push. 
With forecast snow levels rising to over 8000 feet with this front, 
wintry impacts are of little concern. Elevated winds are possible 
but at this point gusts are short of hazard thresholds. Westerly 
flow behind the warm front would allow for additional rainfall along 
the coast and Cascades, with temperatures staying slightly above 
seasonal averages. 

Chances for active weather continue into the weekend, with some 
agreement for a pause on Saturday ahead of a front bringing 
precipitation on Sunday. Long-term meteograms show good agreement 
for most areas to see some rainfall. Weekend snow levels are 
currently forecast to stay above 6000 feet. Meteograms also show 
activity continuing beyond this coming weekend, but relatively 
coarse outcomes offer little certainty in the characteristics of 
future activity. -TAD

AVIATION...23/18Z TAFs...Low ceilings continue late this morning 
in the Rogue and Illinois Valleys but should mix out by about 19-
20Z. For the rest of the day, VFR/MVFR conditions will prevail 
across the region with only partial terrain obscurations of the 
highest peaks.  Scattered showers should be limited to North Bend 
(OTH) and Roseburg (RBG) as a Pacific front moves onshore.

The primary hazard during the TAF period will be the development of 
low level wind shear from west to east this afternoon and evening, 
beginning as early as 21Z at OTH and spreading east of the Coast 
Ranges by 06Z.  Given turbulent mixing, model guidance suggests a 
noticeably drier boundary layer tonight compared to previous nights, 
although low level wind shear will remain a concern throughout the 
region.  If the boundary layer is able to completely decouple 
overnight, scattered low cloud could develop at RBG and Medford 
(MFR), but confidence remains somewhat high that MVFR conditions 
will prevail even in this potential scenario. -Spinetti

MARINE...Updated 200 AM PST Monday, November 23, 2026...Gusty 
south winds and high and steep northwest swell continue this 
morning. This will maintain conditions hazardous to small craft 
into Monday morning before conditions rapidly deteriorate later 
this morning.

A strong front approaches the waters today and gradually moves 
onshore during the day Tuesday. As the front nears, expect south 
winds to increase to gales for all areas this morning. Wind driven 
seas will become very steep and hazardous with these conditions 
persisting into the overnight hours. As the front approaches the 
coast late tonight into Tuesday, expect winds to reach storm force 
of 40 to 50 kt with gusts of 55 to 60 kt for much of the outer 
waters with strong gales persisting for the inner waters. Isolated 
areas of storm force winds are possible for the inner waters, and we 
may need to consider expanding the Storm Warning to the inner waters 
over the coming shifts. Seas will become chaotic and dangerous 
Monday night through much of Tuesday, peaking around 22 to 28 ft 
Tuesday morning/afternoon. 

Conditions ease some late Tuesday into Wednesday as winds briefly 
lower below gales. However seas will remain very steep and high to 
very high as another long period, west swell builds into the waters 
late Tuesday into Wednesday. Another front is expected late 
Wednesday and Thursday, and this system could bring another round of 
strong south winds. Current guidance indicates about a 50% chance of 
another round of gales, but should generally be weaker compared to 
the upcoming system. Overall, expect periods of strong winds with 
very steep, high to very high seas throughout the holiday week. 

COASTAL AND BEACH HAZARDS...Updated 230 PM PST Sunday, November 22, 
2026...Another round of dangerous conditions is expected along the 
coast this week. Higher than normal high tides (King Tides) will be 
present this week. This will bring an increased threat for the 
inundation of low-lying areas along beaches, shorelines and tidal 
waterways of Douglas, Coos and Curry Counties. The main impacts are 
expected during the highest high tides that peak in the late morning 
and early afternoon starting Monday, and likely persisting through 
the end of the week. 

A Coastal Flood Advisory is in place today when up to 2.4 ft of 
inundation above ground level is expected due to these higher than 
normal high tides. This is primarily for the communities of Gold 
Beach, Coos Bay, Charleston and Reedsport as well as portions of 
Highway 101 in the vicinity of those locations. The threat increases 
on Tuesday and Wednesday as King Tides combine with storm surge from 
large surf and brings up to 3.1 ft of inundation during the highest 
high tide periods those days. Additionally, beach conditions will 
become dangerous again Tuesday and Wednesday as large breaking wave 
heights of 23 to 28 ft are expected in the surf zone. A Coastal 
Flood Warning is in place for the whole coastline to account for the 
increased flooding threat and these hazardous beach conditions. 

Storm activity lessens beyond Thursday, but King Tides will still be 
present and this will maintain the threat of coastal flooding 
through at least the end of the week. At the Charleston, OR tide 
gauge, high tide is expected to be at 10:09 AM this morning, at 
10:51 AM Tuesday, at 11:35 AM Wednesday, and at 12:23 PM Thursday.

This event could see impacts similar to what occurred on January 
3rd, 2026. Numerous roads may be closed during this event. Low lying 
property including homes, businesses and some critical 
infrastructure could be inundated and some shoreline erosion will 
occur. Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property. 
If travel is required, do not drive around barricades or through 
water of unknown depth. 

Another factor to consider is that not only are the high tides 
higher than normal, but also the low tides are LOWER than normal. A 
greater difference between high and low tide (known as a large tidal 
range) moves larger volumes of water in and out over the same 
roughly 6-hour window. This creates faster tidal currents, deeper 
water at high tide, and wider exposed areas at low tide. After the 
low tide and water begins to come back in, it comes in much faster 
than usual and this can catch people off guard. Bottom line: don't 
venture out onto beaches at low tide. Stay safe. Stay far away. 

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...

* Cold temperatures and areas of freezing fog this morning,
  followed by mostly dry weather today through Tuesday afternoon.

* A weak storm brings increased winds and light Sierra snow 
  Tuesday night into Wednesday morning. 

* Dry and mild weather is favored for Thanksgiving Day, with
  additional storms possible late next weekend and beyond. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...

Clearing skies and light showers from Sunday evening will support
pockets of freezing fog across NE California and E Sierra valleys
this morning -- including along I-80 near Truckee. Be prepared 
for reduced visibilities and slick roads during this morning's 
commute in these areas before fog mixes out around 9-10 AM PST. 
Today through much of Tuesday will offer dry weather and cool 
temperatures beneath transient high pressure. This will be the 
most ideal window for trans-Sierra travel before light snow 
returns Tuesday night...

A quick upper trough passage will increase shower chances along 
the Sierra from Lassen County to the Tahoe Basin Tuesday evening 
through Wednesday morning. This storm will be a rather weak one, 
providing up to 1" of snow along the Sierra crest and at pass 
level. Even the "snowier" scenarios (10% chance) only show 2-4" 
along highest peaks and along Donner Pass by midday Wednesday. 
Truckee and Lake Tahoe communities may see, at most, a trace of 
snow on grassy and elevated surfaces early Wednesday (10% odds). 
While major travel impacts are not anticipated, those traveling 
through the Sierra should be prepared for slick roads near 
summits. Dry conditions are favored for Mono County and W Nevada 
communities where showers are shadowed out. 

Winds begin to increase on Tuesday as the trough approaches, 
yielding SW gusts of 25-35 mph near the Oregon border and 20-30 mph 
gusts across E Sierra valleys Tuesday afternoon. Ridgetop winds may 
gust up to 80 mph at times. Expect wind impacts to backcountry and 
lake recreation, with turbulent flights into and out of regional 
airports Tuesday into Wednesday morning. 

Aside from a low 10-20% chance of rain near the Oregon border, 
Thanksgiving Day is shaping up to be dry and mild as high pressure 
overspreads the region. Daytime highs are slated to be in the upper 
40s and 50s, followed by chilly nighttime lows in the 20s and 30s 
early Friday morning. Dry weather prevails Friday and much of 
Saturday before the potential for another storm increases Sunday 
into Monday, posing impacts to post-holiday travel plans. This 
storm has a warmer look with higher snow levels keeping snow in 
the mountains and rain in the valleys. Ensembles suggest that 
we'll remain in a stormy pattern next week, but hard to have much 
confidence at this extended range. 

-Salas

&&

Tuesday. Mid to high level clouds begin to increase this afternoon 
ahead of an approaching weak storm. 

Regional Outlook: FZFG will lead to periods of LIFR conditions at 
KTRK through 16-17Z this morning. Otherwise, VFR conditions and 
light breezes prevail through Tuesday morning.   

24-72 Hour Outlook: A weak Pacific storm will increase winds and 
bring light snow showers to Tahoe terminals Tuesday night and 
Wednesday morning. A 20-40% chance of -SN at KTRK-KTVL may reduce 
CIGS/VIS to MVFR conditions Tuesday night into Wednesday morning. SW 
FL100 flow increases to around 35 kts Tuesday afternoon from Tahoe 
northward, posing LLWS and mountain wave turbulence impacts at KTRK-
KTVL and KRNO-KCXP-KMEV into Tuesday night.

National Weather Service Las Vegas NV
1058 AM PST Mon Nov 23 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

* Breezy north winds are expected Wednesday and Thursday across
  the Colorado River Valley. This may result in hazardous boating
  conditions on large inland lakes.

* A noted warming trend is expected the remainder of the week
  through the holiday weekend. 

* The next substantial storm system looks to impact the Western
  U.S. the first half of next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
A rather benign weather pattern is expected through the remainder
of this week and weekend. A pronounced upper ridge will gradually
build in across the Desert Southwest, providing pleasant and mild
weather conditions. Nights will remain cool, but daytime highs 
will gradually climb well into the 60s and 70s from Thursday 
through Saturday.

One area of concern will be the Colorado River Valley, where 
gusty north winds look to develop Wednesday through Thanksgiving 
day. This will occur as a shortwave drops south across western 
Utah and Arizona and the pressure gradient tightens in response to
the intensifying ridge. At this time, winds appear somewhat 
marginal for advisory headlines, but they will likely be enough to
cause problems on large inland lakes. Lake wind and/or wind 
advisories may become necessary in future forecasts.

Beyond the holiday weekend, ensembles are in generally good 
agreement in the handling of another upper trough emanating from 
the Eastern Pacific. While details regarding timing and intensity 
remain, the probability of another round of breezy/gusty southwest
winds, valley rain and mountain snow is on the rise, particularly
in the Monday to Wednesday timeframe next week.

across the Vegas Valley through the forecast period. Speeds will

conditions will prevail, with FEW clouds and bases remaining AOA

For the rest of southern Nevada, northwest Arizona and southeast

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Phoenix AZ
1234 PM MST Mon Nov 23 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Dry and mostly tranquil weather is expected to persist through 
  at least the Thanksgiving Weekend.

- Temperatures will embark on a gradual warming trend over the 
  next several days as high pressure encompasses much of the 
  western United Sates.

- Periods of breezy conditions over high terrain areas and along
  the lower Colorado River Valley will be the only notable
  conditions to speak. 

&&

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/... 
Uneventful weather and seasonal temperatures are expected through
the first half of this week. Current water vapor imagery shows a 
shortwave trough pushing east across AZ. The trough axis has 
already moved east of Phoenix and with its passage high clouds 
have cleared. Shortwave ridging will follow today's trough heading
through tomorrow and then another weak dry trough will drop 
through the area on Wednesday. Overall, increasing H5 heights, up 
to 579-581dam by the end of the day tomorrow, will lead to warming
through the middle of the week. High temperatures this afternoon 
will be similar to yesterday to 1-3F cooler in south-central AZ 
due to the trough passage. Lower desert highs will reach the upper
60s to lower 70s. The warming Tuesday and Wednesday will result in
afternoon highs in the lower to middle 70s. The mornings will
remain very chilly, with mostly 40s and some 30s tomorrow morning
and then 40s to lower 50s Wednesday morning. The pressure gradient
over the area remains weak, which means continue very light winds
today. There will be some increased mountain breeziness tomorrow
morning east of Phoenix and again Wednesday with more coverage
across southern AZ, as surface high pressure builds to the north
and east, but peak gusts will mostly be in the 20-25 mph range.

&&

.LONG TERM /THURSDAY THROUGH NEXT MONDAY/...  
The initial ridge Tuesday will be the starting point for a 
persistent anti-cyclonic setup through Thanksgiving and the ensuing 
weekend. An unseasonably strong area of high pressure is shown 
building to the west of the Baja Peninsula and expanding across 
much of the western CONUS during the back-half of the week. This 
will keep mostly quiet conditions in the forecast during the 
extended period, resulting in what looks to be a wonderful holiday
timeframe weather-wise. Another round of breeziness Thursday, 
this time focused over the lower Colorado River Valley, will once 
again be the deviant factor to the overall benign setup as the 
strong high pressure interacts with the previously mentioned 
shortwave that will be over Northern Mexico by this point in time.

Afternoon highs by Thanksgiving will rise far enough to be 
comfortably above normal values for the back-end of November, but
that will only result in middle to upper 70s becoming more common
across lower elevation areas. There might be a few spots, mainly 
out in SW Arizona and SE California, that reach into the lower 80s
by the weekend due to their closer proximity to the greatest 
height anomalies, but that appears to be the upper limit of how 
far temperatures will rise. With the high centered to our 
southwest, cool northerly flow will likely be an inhibiting factor
as to why we will not see warmth that is completely out of the 
ordinary for this time of year. 

&&

.AVIATION...Updated at 1800Z.

South Central Arizona including KPHX, KIWA, KSDL, and KDVT: 
No major aviation concerns are expected through the TAF period.
Light, variable winds will give way to the typical diurnal pattern
by early afternoon. Clear skies will prevail throughout Monday 
before FEW high clouds develop late tonight.

Southeast California/Southwest Arizona including KIPL and KBLH:
No major aviation concerns are expected through the TAF period.
The light and variable winds from this morning will develop a
distinct northerly component with winds aob 6 kt by 21Z at both
airports, continuing through late tonight before going more W-NW.
This slight wind shift will be accompanied by SCT high clouds 
moving into the region overnight.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER... 
Dry and mostly tranquil conditions will persist through the next
several days. MinRHs will hover around 15-30% areawide, while 
cool overnight lows will allow for decent to good overnight 
recovery. Daily high temperatures are expected to gradually rise 
through the holiday weekend, reaching above seasonal normals as
early as Tuesday or Wednesday, depending on location. Outside of 
some marginally breezy conditions over AZ high terrain areas and 
the lower Colorado River Valley throughout the week, light winds 
will be favored elsewhere.

&&

.HYDROLOGY...Updated 11/23 1933.
Gila RIver: A Flood Warning remains in effect from Painted Rock 
Dam through the Dateland area due to continued water releases 
upwards of 3000 cfs. Water levels near Dateland continue to rise, 
with gauge data now showing a depth of just above 7 ft and flow 
exceeding 1100 cfs. At the current rate of rise, the water level 
at the Dateland gauge is expected to reach action stage (8 ft) by 
Thursday-Friday. A separate Flood Warning segment remains in 
effect from Dateland to Yuma. These water levels will have the 
potential to flood farm fields and low water crossings along the 
river downstream from the dam.
